summary: US-F3: Payees and split schedules - a split that does not sum exactly is refused
description:
**As** a platform operator, **I want** every fee to name who it is owed to and in what share,
**so that** a settlement run has an unambiguous answer for every cent — and **so that** a
misconfigured split is impossible to author rather than discovered at payout.

**Priority:** P0  **Depends on:** TKT-214

Half of TKT-6's second COS: *splits sum exactly to totals*. This ticket owns the **definition and
the allocator**; TKT-217 owns writing the result to the ledger.

**The trap:** shares are percentages, money is whole cents, and the two do not divide. A fee of
1 cent split three ways at 3333/3333/3334 bps floors to 0/0/0 and loses the cent. Every real
ticketing settlement has this bug once. The allocator here is a **pure function with a proof
obligation**: the parts sum to the input exactly, for every input, or the test fails.

**Acceptance Criteria:**
- [ ] A migration adds a payee registry (organizer-scoped: a kind, a display name, an external
  reference) and split schedules keyed by fee code and scope, each part carrying `share_bps`.
  The **write refuses** any split set whose `share_bps` do not sum to exactly 10000 — enforced in
  the database, not only in the handler, so a direct writer cannot author an unbalanced set.
- [ ] `system`, `venue` and `artist` are expressible on day one and the list is **extensible**: a
  new payee is a row, never a migration. Whether a new *kind* is also a row or a checked enum
  change is a plan decision, stated with its reason (the ADR-021 lens: which of the two an
  operator can get wrong, and what happens when they do).
- [ ] A **pure allocator** turns one fee amount into whole-cent payee parts: floor by bps, then
  **largest remainder** with a deterministic, documented tie-break. Property-tested: for every
  amount in a wide range and every split shape under test, `sum(parts) == amount` **exactly** and
  no part is negative. The pathological cases are named tests, not just generated: 1 cent across
  3 payees, amount 0, the contract's maximum `Money` amount, and a two-payee 5000/5000 split of an
  odd amount.
- [ ] Split schedules resolve through the **same hierarchy** as fee rules, per fee code: one
  winning split set per code, same comparator, same provenance shape. A fee code with no split
  schedule resolves to "unsplit" — an explicit state with a reason, never an empty set that reads
  as "split to nobody".
- [ ] The resolved split per fee code is readable through a contract-declared response with
  provenance; regen committed.
- [ ] `make check` green (lint + test + build, Go & TS, gateway smoke suite); regenerated code committed before the gate runs (ADR-009).

**Non-goals:** the settlement ledger and anything written at capture time (TKT-217) · payout
execution, bank details or KYC (not in this epic) · reporting and exports (TKT-23).

objective.note: Every fee code can name its payees and shares, and the arithmetic that turns a share into cents is exact by construction.

scope.note: Definitions + resolution + the pure allocator. Nothing is written to a ledger and no sale changes.

uncertainties.note: (a) payee kind as a checked enum vs a free row; (b) whether splits hang off the fee rule or off the fee code at a scope - the ACs require the hierarchy either way; (c) which service owns payees (catalog holds rule definitions per ADR-002, but a payee is an accounting entity payments may want). The plan decides and the ADR-002 boundary answer is stated explicitly.

dependencies.note: Blocked by TKT-214 - splits key off fee codes and reuse its comparator.

approach.note: Allocator as a pure function next to the comparator, tested by property + named pathological cases. Definition tables mirror fee_rules' scoping so one comparator serves both.

first_slice.note: The allocator is the piece the ledger cannot be written without, and the piece a later fix cannot retroactively repair - already-settled cents stay misallocated.

success.note: Exact-sum property assertions and refusal assertions; both are deterministic.

binding.rule: Money is integer minor units + ISO currency code - floats are banned on money paths.

Local gate: `make check` (lint + test + build, Go & TS, plus the gateway smoke suite; run `make deps` first on a clean clone). CI runs the same gate - keep them mirrored. Commit regenerated code (`openapi_gen.go`, `api-types.gen.ts`) before running the gate - `check-generate` diffs against HEAD, so an uncommitted regen reads as drift and fails the run.

governingAdrs.why: SHIPPED (TKT-214) AND CONSUMED (TKT-215). Fixes the fee model this ticket attaches payees to: fee codes are opaque and case-sensitive, one winner per code, rounding is floor at the individual ticket, incidence is passed_on vs absorbed, and - directly for this ticket - §2 states that A RESOLVED FEE OF AMOUNT 0 IS STILL A RESOLVED FEE, which means a split allocator will be handed zero amounts and must not treat them as absent.

The hierarchy and comparator that fee rules reuse and split schedules will reuse again: five derived scope levels, specificity order, forced-override partition, priority, stable-id tiebreak, and the (scope_level, scope_id) index predicate. Also §3's write-gate pattern for a polymorphic scope with no FK.
Money is integer minor units. The allocator is integer-only: bps shares divide money that does not divide evenly, and the residue must be allocated, never rounded away.

catalog owns rule definitions; payments owns the settlement ledger. A PAYEE is an accounting entity - deciding which service owns it is this ticket's boundary question, and moving the line needs an explicit amendment, not an assertion.
Contract-first: any new operation must be declared and the generated code committed BEFORE the gate.
Response validation fails closed. A new REQUIRED field breaks every pre-existing response; amounts above the Money cap 500 at read time.

A scoped catalog read needs an index behind its filter and TWO tests: the result is scoped AND the scan is. TKT-214 did this for fee_rules; split schedules resolving through the same hierarchy owe the same pair.
Plain CREATE INDEX; CONCURRENTLY is not adopted.
Migrations run out-of-band via each binary's migrate subcommand.
Name the adversary before claiming an integrity property. A sum-to-10000 CHECK is honest-writer consistency, not tamper-evidence - a direct DB writer bypasses it.

Where a service's auth guard lives: declared security guards a public contract, an inline check guards an internal surface. TKT-214 put the fee read on /internal/ because absorbed fees are the organizer's cost structure - SPLIT SHARES ARE STRICTLY MORE SENSITIVE, so the same reasoning applies with more force.

reference.summary: Epic lineage and the three epic-level COS
The fee model, merged: basis kinds, rounding, incidence, channel, the /internal/ read and why
The fee comparator and its per-code partition - split schedules resolve the same way
The write gate for a polymorphic scope with no FK, and the ADR-019 evidence pair

What TKT-215 persists and TKT-217 will settle from: the envelope {resolution, breakdown, face_value, passed_on_fees, absorbed_fees, total_amount}, and the breakdown item shape {fee_code, basis, incidence, amount, currency}
TKT-215 closeout: the fee-on-exchange policy was decided by an agent as 'carried', and refunds under-refund by the passed-on fee. Both bear on what a settlement ledger must eventually reverse

comments.body:
<!-- sdlc:stage=ready kind=claim -->
### Claimed — TKT-216 (US-F3)

**Selection.** TKT-215 closed. TKT-216 is the only remaining claimable child — TKT-217 is still
blocked on it. No tie-break needed.

**Blockers verified:** `blocked-by TKT-214` — resolved (Done, `0d821677`). TKT-216 does not depend on
TKT-215, but it lands after it, which is useful: the breakdown shape a split allocator must consume
now exists rather than being predicted.

**Branch:** `TKT-216-payees-and-splits`, cut from `origin/main` at `a05d5cc6`.

**Risk verdict — `risk:low` NOT claimed.** This ticket decides how money is *attributed*, and its
allocator is the thing TKT-217 settles from. A rounding residue lost here is money that never
reaches a payee, and unlike a display bug it is unrecoverable after the fact. Data migration and
money-path carve-outs both apply.

**Gates waived — same terms as TKT-214 and TKT-215**, restated so this ticket's history stands alone:
Gate 1 by the owner's instruction; Gate 2 replaced by agent judgement after the cross-model critique
(prefer the critique's recommendation, else the most reversible option, every decision recorded in
`kind=plan-final`); Gate 3 replaced by agent squash-merge after the ai-review converges under the
unchanged churn cap, review-guide posted first; Gate 4 replaced by self-validation against test
evidence on merged code.

**Model routing** re-read at claim, unchanged: `plan` = `gpt-5.6-luna` · `planReview` = `main-agent` ·
`implement` = `main-agent` · `aiReview` = `gpt-5.6-luna`. Both cross-model pairs hold.

**Context-mémo re-baked**, applying TKT-214's retro rule (include every ADR of the current week
regardless of area match):

- **ADR-046 promoted to the top** — it is now shipped and consumed, and its §2 clause *"a resolved
  fee of amount 0 is still a resolved fee"* lands directly on this ticket: the allocator will be
  handed zero amounts and must not treat them as absent.
- **ADR-043 added** — TKT-214 put the fee read on `/internal/` because absorbed fees are the
  organizer's cost structure. **Split shares are strictly more sensitive than that**, so the same
  reasoning applies with more force, and the plan should not have to rediscover it.
- **TKT-215's closeout added as a reference** — the fee-on-exchange policy was decided by an agent
  as "carried", and refunds currently under-refund by the passed-on fee. Both bear on what a
  settlement ledger eventually has to reverse, and neither is visible from the code.

**Carried forward from TKT-215's retro, since it recurs here:** the `agent:plan-review` label moves
**before** the critique starts on this ticket, not when its comment is posted — so the cross-model
split is measurable for once.

<!-- sdlc:stage=planning kind=plan -->
### Execution plan — TKT-216 (draft)

**Drafted by `gpt-5.6-luna` (Codex, read-only, effort=high)**, per `config.models.plan`. Condensed;
every cited seam re-verified at HEAD during plan-review.

**Boundary:** catalog holds the payee registry, split-schedule definitions, hierarchy resolution and
contract exposure; payments holds the pure allocator (consumed by TKT-217); commerce validates and
persists the enriched resolution; ledger writes stay out of scope. **ADR-002 unamended**, with a new
ADR-047 recording the clarification.

#### 1. The allocator

Pure, in `services/payments/internal/splits/`. Validates `amount >= 0`, at least one part, each
`share_bps` in `0..10000`, unique payee ids, shares summing to exactly 10000 — *"the database
guarantees the last two for authored schedules, but the pure function must defend itself because
TKT-217 will consume persisted snapshots."*

Algorithm: sort by ascending payee UUID (never mutate caller order) · `base_i` and `remainder_i` per
part · `residue = amount − Σbase_i` · one cent each to the `residue` largest remainders · ties by
ascending payee UUID · return sorted by UUID. **Result is therefore independent of input order**, and
UUID is the only stable identity available — display name, external reference and row order can all
change. Mirrors the stable-id tie-break in `feeBeats`.

**Do not form `amount × share_bps`.** Use the same quotient/remainder decomposition as `feeFromRate`:
`q = amount/10000`, `r = amount%10000`, `base = q×bps + (r×bps)/10000`,
`remainder = (r×bps)%10000`. `q×bps <= amount` and `r×bps <= 99,990,000`, so neither multiplication
overflows. **And do not cap internal arithmetic at `maxContractAmount`** — the existing code
distinguishes the contract's Money bound from commerce's int64 composition range.

Worked cases: amount 0 → every payee gets 0, the fee is not omitted · 1¢ at 3333/3333/3334 → all
floors zero, the residue cent goes to the 3334 payee · 1¢ at 5000/5000 → equal remainders, lowest
UUID wins · `maxContractAmount` → still exact, including an odd 5000/5000.

#### 2. Persistence

Catalog migration `0017`: `payee_kinds` (seeded `system`/`venue`/`artist`), `payees`,
`split_schedules` (scope, fee code, channel, priority, forced, window), `split_schedule_parts`.
Organizer-scoped **composite** foreign keys so a schedule cannot reference another organizer's payee;
unique `(schedule_id, payee_id)`; the same polymorphic write gate as `feeRuleWriteGateQuery`.

Balance enforced by a **deferred constraint trigger**: a header with no parts fails at commit, any
part change rechecks the total, and the sum must be exactly 10000. Temporary imbalance is legal only
inside the uncommitted transaction. Honest-writer consistency, not tamper-evidence (ADR-021).

**Kinds are rows, not an enum** — a typo cannot silently route money because the referenced kind must
exist, and a new kind is data. The residual risk is classification, not arithmetic. TKT-217 must
treat kind as descriptive metadata, never as an implicit routing rule.

#### 3. Resolution and exposure

**Extend the existing fee-resolution response** rather than adding a second read. Each
`FeeCodeResolution` gains `split{resolver_version, mode: split|unsplit, reason, winner, candidates}`.
A code with no schedule serializes `mode: unsplit, reason: no_schedule, winner: null, candidates: []`
— *"materially different from an empty part list"*. A schedule outside its window is `unsplit` with a
distinct reason and retained loser provenance.

Same five levels, same filters, forced partition, specificity, priority and stable-id tie-break as
the fee resolver; the candidate read matches `(scope_level, scope_id)` pairs. **Endpoint stays
`/internal/`, 401, `no-store`** — split shares are more sensitive than absorbed fee amounts, so
publishing them would reverse ADR-046 §6.

#### 4–6. Files, tests, risks

New: ADR-047 · migration 0017 · `store/splits.go`, `store/splits_postgres.go` ·
`payments/internal/splits/`. Extended: `store/fees.go`, `fees_postgres.go`, `api/fees.go`, the
contract + regen, and (per the draft) commerce's consumer.

Tests to observe failing first: an exact-sum **property test whose oracle uses `math/big` and must
not call allocator helpers or reuse its arithmetic** — explicitly following the independent-oracle
pattern TKT-215's review forced · named cases (1¢/3 payees, zero, maximum, odd 5000/5000, input-order
independence) · a DB test committing `3333+3333+3333` and asserting **Commit fails**, then
`3333+3333+3334` succeeding — *"a test inserting only one part would fail because of the
empty-schedule guard, not because the sum rule works"* · resolution provenance across two codes, one
with no schedule · the ADR-019 poison-row and index-scoped pair.

<!-- sdlc:stage=plan-review kind=plan -->
### Adversarial plan critique — TKT-216

**By `main-agent` (Claude Opus 5)**, per `config.models.planReview`.

#### Seam verification at HEAD — clean

`fees.go` comparator and per-code partition · `feeBeats` stable-id tie-break · `feeRuleWriteGateQuery`
· the pair-matching candidate query · `feeFromRate` and its decomposition · the int64-vs-Money-cap
distinction · `explainGenericPlan` · the ADR-019 evidence pair · ADR-046 §6's internal decision ·
migration 0014's verbatim `resolution` — **all exist and say what the draft says they say.**

**This draft is materially better than the last two**, and specifically because it read the previous
tickets' scars: it cites `feeFromRate`, warns against forming `amount × share_bps`, warns against
capping at `maxContractAmount`, and demands an independent `big.Int` oracle — all three of which were
review findings on TKT-215. The mémo carrying TKT-215's closeout forward did what it was supposed to.

**Self-refutation check: clean.** No Con in the draft negates its own recommendation.

#### ⛔ A1 [blocking] — delete the commerce changes; they are unnecessary AND harmful

The draft has commerce *"decode and validate the split state before the hold"*. Both halves are wrong.

**Unnecessary — verified empirically, not argued.** `storableSnapshot` decodes into a generic `any`
and re-encodes, so unknown fields survive verbatim. I ran it against a document carrying a `split`
object:

```
in : {"resolver_version":1,"fees":[],"split":{"mode":"split","parts":[{"payee_id":"x","share_bps":5000}]}}
out: {"fees":[],"resolver_version":1,"split":{"mode":"split","parts":[{"payee_id":"x","share_bps":5000}]}}
```

The snapshot already carries splits with **zero** commerce changes. That is not an accident — it is
the property `catalog_pricing.go` documents at length as the reason `DisallowUnknownFields` was
rejected.

**Harmful — it would let a payout misconfiguration refuse a ticket sale.** Commerce validating splits
means an unbalanced or missing schedule fails the reserve. Splits decide *who gets paid afterwards*;
the buyer's purchase does not depend on them. Wiring settlement configuration into the sale's
fail-closed path converts a back-office data error into **lost sales**, on the hot path, for a
property this ticket does not need. TKT-217 validates splits where they are used — at settlement,
where refusing costs a retry rather than a customer.

**Amendment: commerce is not touched by this ticket.** Drop `catalog_fees.go` and its test from the
file list.

#### ⛔ A2 [blocking] — state the snapshot reason, because it is the load-bearing one

The draft extends the existing response rather than adding a second read, and justifies it as "one
read". Correct choice, **wrong reason**, and the right reason changes what must be tested.

The load-bearing property is that TKT-215's snapshot stores catalog's document **verbatim**. Putting
the split inside that document means the split is captured *at sale time* — so a schedule edited
afterwards cannot change who gets paid for a sale that already happened. That is the same
snapshot-not-reference discipline migration 0006 and 0014 both argue for, and it is the reason
TKT-217 can settle truthfully at all.

A second endpoint would have satisfied "resolution is readable" while silently leaving settlement to
re-resolve later against mutated schedules. **The plan must say this**, and owe one test: a split
schedule changed *after* a reserve must not change that reservation's stored split.

#### A3 [minor] — drop `currency` from `split_schedules`

Shares are basis points, which are currency-independent. A column no code reads invites a
mismatch check nobody needs, and TKT-214 already pays for one currency check per fee rule because
there it is load-bearing. Here it is not.

#### A4 [minor] — name the trigger's escape hatch precisely

*"Direct SQL cannot commit an unbalanced schedule unless trigger enforcement is deliberately
disabled"* is right but vague. ADR-021 asks for the adversary in words: a writer with
`session_replication_role = replica` or `ALTER TABLE … DISABLE TRIGGER` bypasses it entirely. So this
is **honest-writer consistency** — it stops an operator mistake, not an adversary — and the ADR must
say so in those terms rather than implying the database makes imbalance impossible.

#### Accepted

The allocator in full — algorithm, decomposition, tie-break by payee UUID, order independence, the
four worked cases, and both "do not" warnings · payees and kinds as rows with composite
organizer-scoped FKs · the deferred constraint trigger · unsplit as an explicit state with a reason ·
`/internal/` + 401 + `no-store` · ADR-047 · the independent-oracle requirement and the
three-part unbalanced fixture (the draft's own note that a one-part fixture would fail for the wrong
reason is exactly right) · the ADR-019 pair.

#### Sizing — CONCERNS, stated rather than fixed

Even after A1 removes commerce, this is four new tables, a trigger, two new store files, a new
payments package, changes to three existing catalog files, the contract, and six test groups. It will
land well above the ~400-line guideline. I am **not** splitting it, because every AC is load-bearing
and a split would produce a schema-only ticket that reaches Gate 4 with nothing to demonstrate —
which `decomposition.md` names as the failure mode to avoid. Recording it as a known cost.

#### Pre-mortem

*Assume the PR bounced.* (1) A payout misconfiguration blocks a sale → **A1**. (2) Settlement pays
the wrong payee because the schedule changed after the sale → **A2**'s test. (3) The property test's
oracle mirrors the implementation and proves nothing → the draft already forbids it; keep it.
(4) The exact-sum property fails at `maxContractAmount` → the decomposition is verified below.
(5) A gate run is lost to lint or a registry test → run module tests **and** `golangci-lint` before
the gate (TKT-215's retro, now applied twice).

Lens changed the plan in two places (A1, A2).

#### Independent verification of the allocator, before implementation

I implemented the draft's algorithm separately and checked it against a direct oracle: **exact sum
holds** across the boundary set and **50,000 random (shape, amount) pairs up to `MaxInt64`**, no
part negative, and the residue is always `< len(parts)`. Neither multiplication overflowed. The
specification is sound; what remains is whether the Go implementation matches it, which is what the
independent-oracle property test is for.

<!-- sdlc:stage=planning kind=plan-final -->
### Plan final — TKT-216

**The `kind=plan` draft, as amended below, is the plan.** Delta only.

#### Amendments

**A1** Commerce is not touched — the snapshot already carries splits verbatim (verified), and
validating them there would let a payout misconfiguration refuse a sale.
**A2** The reason for extending the existing response is the **snapshot**, not read-count; owes a
test that a schedule edited after a reserve does not change that reservation's stored split.
**A3** No `currency` on `split_schedules`.
**A4** The trigger's guarantee is honest-writer consistency, with `session_replication_role` and
`DISABLE TRIGGER` named as the escape.

#### Decisions made by the agent because Gate 2 is waived

| # | Decision | Rule | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| D1 | Payees + schedules in **catalog**; allocator in **payments**; ADR-002 unamended | critique recommends | Schedules are organizer-scoped configuration resolved through catalog's hierarchy; the allocator is consumed by the ledger. Recorded in ADR-047 |
| D2 | Kinds are **rows**, not an enum | critique recommends | A typo cannot route money — the FK must resolve. Residual risk is classification, not arithmetic |
| D3 | Split rides the **existing** fee resolution | critique recommends, reason corrected by A2 | Puts the split inside the sale-time snapshot, so a later schedule edit cannot rewrite a past sale |
| D4 | Endpoint stays `/internal/`, 401, `no-store` | critique recommends | Split shares are strictly more sensitive than absorbed fees; publishing them reverses ADR-046 §6 |
| D5 | Balance by **deferred constraint trigger** | most reversible | Enforced for every writer, not just the handler, as AC 1 demands; relaxing later is additive |
| D6 | `unsplit` is an explicit state with a reason | most reversible | "Considered and nothing applies" vs "no such code" must stay distinguishable, exactly as ADR-046 §9 required for fees |

#### Introduced at plan-review, reviewed by no second model

**A1, A2, A3, A4.** A1 is the consequential one: it *removes* work the drafter proposed, on the
judgement that coupling the sale's fail-closed path to payout configuration trades availability for
nothing. If that judgement is wrong the cost is that TKT-217 discovers a bad split later, at
settlement — which is where it is cheap to discover.

#### Test seam

The pure allocator in `services/payments/internal/splits/`, plus the per-code split selector beside
`SelectFeeRules`. Both are pure and table-driven, matching the seam TKT-214 established.

#### Sizing

**CONCERNS, accepted.** Above the ~400-line guideline even after A1. Not split, because every AC is
load-bearing and the alternative is a schema-only ticket with nothing to demonstrate at Gate 4.

#### Gate 2

Waived. Proceeding to `Building` with six decisions and four unreviewed amendments named.

<!-- sdlc:stage=coding kind=summary -->
### Implementation — TKT-216

**Implemented by `main-agent` (Claude Opus 5)**, per `config.models.implement`. PR
[#176](https://github.com/mathd/ticketing_system/pull/176), 1 commit.

```yaml
stage: coding
implementer: main-agent (Claude Opus 5)
pr: 176
gate_runs: 2 (1 red for a PRE-EXISTING flake, 1 green)
mutation_checks: 7
```

#### TDD

`Allocate` was stubbed and the whole suite observed red — every pathological case, the property
sweep, the order-independence check — before the logic existed.

**Seven mutation checks**, each killed by the intended test: dropping the residue distribution ·
forming `amount × share_bps` directly · tie-break by input order · accepting an unbalanced set ·
collapsing the two unsplit reasons · leaking another channel's schedule into provenance · treating
the forced partition as a tie-break.

#### The mutation check that found a fixture gap

The forced-partition mutant **passed**. That was not a false alarm — it exposed a real hole: my only
forced case was *forced broader vs unforced narrower*, and that gives the **same winner** whether the
partition is a filter or a tie-break (the inverted scope order hands it to the broader rule either
way). The distinguishing case is *forced **narrower** vs unforced **broader***. Added; the mutant now
dies on it.

This is the "fixture too small" failure mode, caught by mutation rather than by reading — and it is
the second time on this epic that the forced partition specifically has needed an extra row to be
observable at all.

#### The mistake I repeated

One mutation reported "no failure" because **it did not compile** (unused variables after the edit)
and my grep hid the build error. Identical in shape to TKT-215's, where I wrote the learning
*"a mutation check that does not compile is not a check"* — one ticket ago. Writing it down did not
change my behaviour; running `go vet` on the mutant before reading the result does, and that is now
how I run them.

#### Deviation from the approved plan

**Commerce is not touched**, per plan-review A1 — and the empirical check is worth recording because
it turned a proposal into a deletion:

```
in : {"resolver_version":1,"fees":[],"split":{"mode":"split","parts":[{"payee_id":"x","share_bps":5000}]}}
out: {"fees":[],"resolver_version":1,"split":{"mode":"split","parts":[{"payee_id":"x","share_bps":5000}]}}
```

The snapshot carries splits with zero changes. Validating them in commerce would additionally have
let a **payout misconfiguration refuse a ticket sale**.

#### Gate

Two runs. The first was red on `web/storefront/test/page-call-budget.test.ts` — **pre-existing**,
proved by reproducing all three failures at the parent commit (a docs-only change on a green gate)
and by passing 6/6 twice at `--testTimeout=30000`. Filed as **TKT-218** rather than fixed here, and
filed with a real question attached: one of the three counts **two** upstream calls where the budget
allows one, so that assertion **fails open** under load and raising the timeout alone would hide it.

Second run green (`EXIT=0`, zero `Error|FAIL|drifted` lines).

<!-- sdlc:stage=ai-review kind=summary -->
### Adversarial review — TKT-216

**By `gpt-5.6-luna` (Codex `adversarial-review`)**, per `config.models.aiReview`. **Two passes**, diff
only. **2 findings, both `[high]`, both fixed.** 1 → 1.

#### Both findings were integrity escapes that no foreign key would catch

**Pass 1 — a part MOVED between schedules validated only its destination.**

```
A={P1:5000,P2:5000}   B={P3:5000,P4:5000}
move P2 A→B    (validates B, now 15000)
delete B/P4    (validates B, now 10000 — passes)
commit         → A commits at 5000, never checked
```

The trigger read `COALESCE(NEW.schedule_id, OLD.schedule_id)`, which on an UPDATE is **always the
destination**. Catalog would then have resolved and snapshotted A, and the allocator would refuse it
as `ErrUnbalanced` — sold fees that settlement cannot allocate.

**Pass 2 — `TRUNCATE` fires no row-level trigger at all.** One statement left every header with zero
parts and committed, bypassing everything above it.

**I reproduced both against a real database before fixing either**, and promoted both into regression
tests. Both mutants (reverting the trigger to destination-only; removing the TRUNCATE guard) fail
with the exact diagnostic.

**What is worth learning from pass 2 specifically:** payments had **already solved** the TRUNCATE
problem on its append-only journal (`0001_journal.sql`, `journal_no_truncate`). I wrote a new
integrity trigger in the same codebase without checking how the existing one was built. The fix is a
copy of that pattern.

#### My own probes, run before the reviewer reported

I attacked the fixed trigger myself with the shapes pass 2 was briefed on: an in-place `share_bps`
update to an unbalanced value (**refused**), a swap between two schedules that unbalances both
(**refused**), empty-then-refill inside one transaction (**committed, balanced** — correct, that is
what deferred means), and emptying a schedule and leaving it (**refused**). Only TRUNCATE got through,
which is the finding.

#### ADR-047 corrected

The ADR claimed the balance rule was *"a property of the database rather than of one code path"*.
Before these two fixes that was worth measurably less than it read. It now records both escapes,
because both looked like the guarantee held and neither was a foreign-key violation.

#### Mutation checks — 9 total

Seven on the implementation (residue distribution · forming the product directly · tie-break by
input order · accepting an unbalanced set · collapsing the unsplit reasons · leaking another
channel's schedule · the forced partition as a tie-break) and two on the fixes (destination-only
trigger · missing TRUNCATE guard).

**(1) What would have made this ticket faster or better?**

  *blocking-but-not-ours*: an incidental finding that **fails the gate** cannot be deferred, because
  deferring it means shipping red. Fix it minimally, file the substantive question separately, and
  record both in the closeout. That is what I ended up doing; the skill should say so rather than
  leaving it to be improvised under pressure.
- **Both `[high]` findings were in trigger logic I wrote from first principles** while an equivalent,
  battle-tested trigger sat in `services/payments`. **Concrete change:** the planning brief's
